doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: Allowing fans to tape concerts and the live-touring business model
summary: The band allowed taping from the start, inspired by Phish and old tapes of Charlie Parker and Bill Monroe. Fleck argues a live touring base is a better business plan than record sales.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Was it a hard decision to basically allow and almost encourage people to tape you in your concerts?

No, I mean I think we just decided to do it right at the beginning, that we just decided to allow it. And it was a time when that was sort of starting to happen. And I guess Phish was an example to me. They were starting to build a huge audience and they were allowing taping and that seemed to be part of it, the Grateful Dead thing the whole sort of jam band thing was just starting. And it seemed like a neat thing to do. And plus we were all, being musicians that study a lot of a old music, we loved the fact that there are tapes of Charlie Parker and there are tapes of cool bluegrass bands, Bill Monroe, and Flatt & Scruggs and you name it. You know Chick Corea live videos. We love all that kind of stuff. So we were thinking how can we love all that stuff and tell people they couldn’t have that of us? And then plus we found that we were playing so differently from night to night, it was cool if somebody showed up with a tape of a show from two years ago and we heard it, we’d go, “hey, that was cool.” You know. I’m glad somebody got that. Because it’s gone, it’s into the ether and it’s gone. So and then plus gradually you start to realize that a concert is a very personal thing for that night for that audience that’s sitting there that night. That’s what that concert is for. They’re connected to it and it’s cool for them to walk away with a version of it if they can get a hold of it, that’s cool. But later when I got to know the guys in Phish and I found that they questioned their own decision to do that because they had a hard time having successful records because people traded the live tapes and then when they put out a record people would say, “oh that’s just slick stuff they’re trying to sell records with.” And so they would have trouble and they weren’t selling the kind of records that they wanted to sell and yet they were selling out Madison Square Garden. Which made me — I looked at that from the outside and I went, “you’re a success. Your live show is an incredible success and it’s just not following the normal template where it’s about record sales and hit records. Your success is about drawing an audience and the way you got there was by trading these live tapes.” And not only that in most cases people don’t make money from their records anyway. The record company is funneling it off one way or another. The more success you have the more videos you do, the more costs come. But if your success is based on live touring nobody can take live touring money away from you. So it’s actually a better business plan to build a great live touring base than to build a great record selling base. And so I just think © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
anything that encourages the live touring base, if you enjoy playing and you like going out and touring, then it’s a wiser business plan with more longevity.
